title: LLM Inference Challenges - Understanding Data Parallelism
author: Anurag Mohan

blocks.text: Understanding Data Parallelism

In the previous parts, we explored why a single GPU is not enough, how tensor parallelism splits tensors across GPUs, and how pipeline parallelism splits layers across stages. At this point, the multi-GPU picture starts becoming much clearer.
But one major question still remains.
Even after distributing the model across many GPUs, how do we actually serve thousands or even millions of users?
That is where data parallelism comes in.
What problem are we solving now?
Tensor parallelism and pipeline parallelism help us run very large models. They solve the problem of model size and computation distribution.
But they do not fully solve concurrency.
Even if a model runs across many GPUs:

requests still queue up
decode is still sequential
KV cache keeps growing
users still compete for the same serving instance
So the next challenge becomes:
How do we scale to many concurrent users?
What does a real multi-GPU setup look like?
Let us build this step by step.
Suppose we have a very large model with 80 layers.
And suppose:

one layer itself is too large for one GPU
the full model is also too large for one GPU
and finally we also want to support many users
Now we need all three techniques together.
Step 1 — What does tensor parallelism look like?
Suppose one layer contains a huge weight matrix like:
One GPU may not have enough memory or compute power.
So we split the tensor across GPUs.
Example:

GPU 1 → first part of weights
GPU 2 → second part
GPU 3 → third part
GPU 4 → fourth part
Now all 4 GPUs cooperate on:

the same layer
the same request
the same computation
So instead of:
1 GPU handling the layer
we now have:
4 GPUs handling one layer together
This is tensor parallelism.
What problem does tensor parallelism solve?
It mainly solves:
How do we run very large layers?
It helps:

fit larger tensors
distribute compute
reduce memory pressure
But notice something important.
All 4 GPUs are still focused on:

the same request
the same model instance
So this alone does not massively increase concurrency.
Step 2 — What does pipeline parallelism look like?
Now suppose the model has:
80 transformer layers
Even with tensor parallelism, the entire model may still not fit efficiently.
So now we split the layers into stages.
Example:

Stage 1 → Layers 1–20
Stage 2 → Layers 21–40
Stage 3 → Layers 41–60
Stage 4 → Layers 61–80
Now combine this with tensor parallelism.
Suppose:

each stage uses 4 GPUs
those GPUs work together using tensor parallelism
Now the setup becomes:

Stage 1 → GPUs 1–4
Stage 2 → GPUs 5–8
Stage 3 → GPUs 9–12
Stage 4 → GPUs 13–16
Now one request flows like this:

Input
→ Stage 1 GPUs
→ Stage 2 GPUs
→ Stage 3 GPUs
→ Stage 4 GPUs
→ Output
So:

pipeline parallelism splits the layers
tensor parallelism splits the tensors inside those layers
Together:

16 GPUs cooperate
to serve ONE model instance
Does this solve concurrency now?
Not completely.
Even though 16 GPUs are involved:

they are still serving the same model instance
users still share the same serving pipeline
decode is still sequential
requests still compete for compute and KV cache
So tensor + pipeline parallelism mainly solve:
How do we run a huge model?
Not:
How do we serve huge numbers of users?
That is where data parallelism enters.
Step 3 — What does data parallelism look like?
Now we create multiple copies of that entire 16-GPU setup.
Example:

Replica 1 → GPUs 1–16
Replica 2 → GPUs 17–32
Replica 3 → GPUs 33–48
Replica 4 → GPUs 49–64
Each replica contains:

the same weights
the same architecture
the same tensor parallel setup
the same pipeline stages
Now requests can be distributed.
Example:

Batch 1 → Replica 1
Batch 2 → Replica 2
Batch 3 → Replica 3
Batch 4 → Replica 4
Or:

Users A–D → Replica 1
Users E–H → Replica 2
Users I–L → Replica 3
Users M–P → Replica 4
Now multiple batches and decode loops can run independently.
THIS is what increases concurrency.
Why does data parallelism solve concurrency?
Because replicas are independent.
Each replica has:

its own weights
its own KV cache
its own scheduler
its own batches
its own decode loop
So instead of one giant serving pipeline:
we now have multiple independent serving pipelines
This scales throughput much more effectively.
How are user sessions managed?
Once a request is assigned to a replica, it usually stays there.
Why?
Because the KV cache for that request already exists inside that replica.
If the request suddenly moves elsewhere:

the new replica would not have the KV cache
attention history would be missing
generation would break or require expensive transfer
So systems usually use:

sticky sessions
or
session affinity
Meaning:
one user stays attached to one replica during generation
What does a practical GPU cluster look like?
At a high level, a GPU cluster is simply many servers connected together.
Each server may contain:

CPUs
RAM
multiple GPUs
networking hardware
storage
Example:

Server
├── CPU
├── RAM
├── 8 GPUs
├── NVLink connections
└── Network interfaces
How are GPUs connected inside one server?
Inside the same machine:

GPUs communicate using NVLink or NVSwitch
bandwidth is extremely high
latency is very low
Example:

GPU ↔ GPU
Very high-speed communication
This is why tensor parallel GPUs are often placed inside the same server.
Because tensor parallelism requires constant GPU-to-GPU communication.
What does a larger cluster look like?
Now suppose one server is not enough.
We connect many servers together.
Example:

Rack 1
├── Server A → 8 GPUs
├── Server B → 8 GPUs
├── Server C → 8 GPUs

Rack 2
├── Server D → 8 GPUs
├── Server E → 8 GPUs
├── Server F → 8 GPUs
Now we may have:
48 GPUs total
connected into one cluster.
How do all three techniques work together in practice?
Suppose we build this setup:

4 pipeline stages
Each stage uses 8 GPUs with tensor parallelism
That becomes:
4 × 8 = 32 GPUs
This entire 32-GPU setup becomes:
ONE model replica
Now suppose we create 4 such replicas:

Replica 1 → Servers 1–4
Replica 2 → Servers 5–8
Replica 3 → Servers 9–12
Replica 4 → Servers 13–16
Now:

tensor parallelism splits tensors
pipeline parallelism splits layers
data parallelism scales concurrent users
This is very close to how large production inference systems operate.
What does request flow look like in practice?
At this point, let us connect everything together into one real inference flow.
Suppose a user sends a prompt like:
"Explain quantum computing..."
The request first reaches a router or load balancer.
The router decides:

which replica should handle the request
which replica currently has capacity
where batching and memory usage look healthy
Example:

Load Balancer
    ↓
Replica 2 selected
Now remember:

Replica 2 itself may contain multiple pipeline stages
each stage may contain multiple GPUs using tensor parallelism
Suppose Replica 2 looks like this:

Stage 1 → GPUs 17–24
Stage 2 → GPUs 25–32
Stage 3 → GPUs 33–40
Stage 4 → GPUs 41–48
Now the request flows through the model step by step.
Example:

Input Prompt
    ↓
Stage 1 GPUs
(tensor parallel computation)
    ↓
Intermediate output
    ↓
Stage 2 GPUs
    ↓
Intermediate output
    ↓
Stage 3 GPUs
    ↓
Stage 4 GPUs
    ↓
Generated token
Inside each stage:

multiple GPUs cooperate using tensor parallelism
partial computations are combined
activations are exchanged between GPUs
Then:

pipeline stages pass outputs forward
the final token is generated
KV cache is updated inside that replica
For the next token:

the request usually stays on the same replica
because the KV cache already exists there
This process repeats token by token during generation.
So at a high level:

Load Balancer
    ↓
Model Replica
    ↓
Pipeline Stages
    ↓
Tensor Parallel GPUs
    ↓
Generated Tokens
This is very close to what happens inside modern large-scale inference systems.
What is the key intuition?
Tensor Parallelism:
Split tensors
Pipeline Parallelism:
Split layers
Data Parallelism:
Replicate the entire model
Together, they make large-scale LLM inference possible.
Why is this article important?
At this point, we have built the complete foundation for understanding modern inference systems.
We now understand:

KV cache
batching
memory pressure
GPU utilization
tensor parallelism
pipeline parallelism
data parallelism
practical GPU clusters
request routing and session affinity
Honestly, this may be one of the most important parts of the series.
Before moving to the next stage, I would strongly recommend revisiting Articles 1–7 one more time.
I am personally doing the same.
As I started exploring the next phase of inference systems, I realized that if these concepts are not extremely clear, the next topics become very difficult to understand intuitively.
I have already gone through these concepts multiple times myself just to build a clearer mental model of what is actually happening inside modern inference systems.
What comes next?
Now that the multi-GPU foundation is much clearer, we can start exploring the next layer of real-world inference systems.
This includes topics like:

distributed serving
request routing
vLLM architecture
paged attention
disaggregated inference
continuous batching across replicas
multi-node communication
advanced serving optimizations
And this is where things start becoming even more interesting.
